title: Regular Expressions
blurb: Search, check and pull apart text with patterns: player names, chat commands, dice rolls and log files.
intro:
A regular expression (regex for short) is a tiny pattern language for text. Instead of asking "does this string contain sword?", you can ask "does it contain a slash, a word, a space and a number?" in one line.

In JavaScript a regex lives between two slashes, like /sword/. If you've used Lua, regex is a bigger cousin of Lua patterns: Lua's %d is regex's \d. Godot has a RegEx class that uses the same syntax you'll learn here.

You'll start with simple checks, then build up to validating player names, reading chat commands like /give sword 3, decoding dice like 2d6+3, and parsing a game log.

Tip

Regex looks scary because it's dense, not because it's hard. Read a pattern one piece at a time, left to right, and it stops being a wall of symbols.

stages.reqMsg: Use a regex and its test() method.
stages.l:
A regex is written between slashes. Its test() method answers one question: does this pattern appear anywhere in the text? It returns true or false.

const pattern = /orc/;
pattern.test("An orc appears");   // true
pattern.test("A goblin appears"); // false
pattern.test("Orc");              // false, capital O

By default a regex is case-sensitive, so O and o are different letters.
stages.p: Return true if text contains sword (lowercase), otherwise false.
stages.h: Write the word between slashes to make a regex, then call its .test(text) method, like /shield/.test(s).

stages.l:
Some characters have special meanings in a pattern. The most common one is . which means any single character. So /.sav/ matches "esav" too!

To mean a real dot, put a backslash in front: \.. This is called escaping. The special characters are:

.  *  +  ?  ^  $  (  )  [  ]  {  }  |  \  /
/a.c/.test("abc");    // true, . matches b
/a\.c/.test("abc");   // false
/a\.c/.test("a.c");   // true
stages.p: Return true if name contains .sav with a real dot.

stages.l:
Square brackets make a character class: match one character from the set.

PatternMatches one...
[aeiou]vowel
[a-z]lowercase letter (a range)
[A-Za-z0-9]letter or digit
[^0-9]character that is not a digit

A ^ right after [ flips the class to mean "anything except these".

/[^a-z]/.test("hello");   // false, all lowercase
/[^a-z]/.test("hello!");  // true, ! is not a-z
stages.p: Return true if name contains any character that is not a letter or a digit.

stages.l:
Some classes are so common they have shortcuts:

ShortcutMeansSame as
\ddigit[0-9]
\wword character[A-Za-z0-9_]
\swhitespacespace, tab, newline

Capital letters flip them: \D is "not a digit", \W "not a word character", \S "not whitespace".
stages.p: ch is one character. Return "digit" if it's a digit, else "word" if it's a word character, else "space" if it's whitespace, else "other".
stages.h: Check digits first, because digits are also word characters: if (/\d/.test(ch)) return "digit";

stages.l:
A quantifier says how many times the thing before it repeats.

  • + means one or more
  • * means zero or more
/\d+/.test("hp 250");    // true, one or more digits
/go*al/.test("gal");     // true, zero o's is fine with *
/go+al/.test("gal");     // false, + needs at least one
/go+al/.test("gooooal"); // true
stages.p: Return true if text contains an x followed by one or more digits, like x12.

stages.l:
? means optional: the thing before it appears zero or one time.

/hp?/.test("h");      // true
/hp?/.test("hp");     // true
/armou?r/.test("armor");  // true
/armou?r/.test("armour"); // true

Handy for British and American spellings!
stages.p: Return true if text contains color or colour.

stages.l:
Curly braces give an exact count or a range:

PatternMeans
a{3}exactly 3 a's
a{2,4}2 to 4 a's
a{2,}2 or more a's
/\d{3}/.test("Room 42");   // false, only 2 digits in a row
/\d{3}/.test("Room 420");  // true
stages.p: Return true if text contains 3 or more ! in a row.

stages.l:
So far, a pattern could match anywhere in the text. Anchors pin it down:

  • ^ means the start of the text
  • $ means the end of the text
/\d{3}/.test("abc1234");     // true, 3 digits somewhere
/^\d{3}$/.test("abc1234");   // false
/^\d{3}$/.test("123");       // true, the WHOLE text is 3 digits

Wrapping a pattern in ^ and $ is how you check that a whole string has the right shape.
stages.p: Return true only if code is exactly 4 digits and nothing else.

stages.reqMsg: Use the i flag after the closing slash.
stages.l:
Letters after the closing slash are flags that change how the pattern behaves. The i flag makes it ignore upper and lower case.

/orc/.test("ORC");    // false
/orc/i.test("ORC");   // true
/orc/i.test("oRc");   // true
stages.p: Return true if text mentions dragon in any mix of capitals.

stages.l:
Round brackets ( ) make a group that remembers what it matched. text.match(pattern) returns an array: item 0 is the whole match, item 1 is the first group, and so on. If nothing matches, you get null.

const m = "Gold: 250".match(/Gold: (\d+)/);
console.log(m[0]);          // "Gold: 250"
console.log(m[1]);          // "250", still a string
console.log(Number(m[1]));  // 250

"Nothing here".match(/Gold: (\d+)/);  // null
stages.p: Return the number after Level as a number, or 0 if there's no match. Capital L only.
stages.h: Use text.match with a regex that captures digits in brackets, like /Score (\d+)/. If there's a match, turn m[1] into a number with Number, otherwise return 0.

stages.l:
Normally a regex stops at the first match. The g flag (global) finds every match. With g, match() returns an array of all the matched strings, or null if there were none.

"a1 b22 c333".match(/\d+/g);   // ["1", "22", "333"]
"abc".match(/\d+/g);           // null
Tip

text.match(/x/g) || [] turns that null into an empty array, so you can safely .map() it.
stages.p: Return all the whole numbers in text as an array of numbers. Return [] if there are none.
stages.h: Match \d+ with the g flag to get every number. match gives null when nothing matches, so fall back to [] with ||, then .map(Number).

stages.l:
text.replace(pattern, newText) swaps matches for something else. Without g it only replaces the first match. Flags can be combined, like gi.

"lag lag lag".replace(/lag/, "win");    // "win lag lag"
"lag LAG lag".replace(/lag/gi, "win");  // "win win win"
stages.p: Replace every darn in any mix of capitals with ****.

stages.reqMsg: Use $1 and $2 in the replacement string.
stages.l:
In a replacement string, $1 means "whatever group 1 matched", $2 is group 2, and so on. This lets you rearrange text.

"Stark, Arya".replace(/(\w+), (\w+)/, "$2 $1");   // "Arya Stark"
"3x5".replace(/(\d+)x(\d+)/, "$1 by $2");         // "3 by 5"
stages.p: Turn every name=number into name: number. For example "hp=10 mp=5" becomes "hp: 10 mp: 5".

stages.l:
split() can take a regex instead of a plain string. That's great for messy input where people type commas, spaces, or both.

"1  2   3".split(" ");      // ["1", "", "2", "", "", "3"]  ugh
"1  2   3".split(/\s+/);    // ["1", "2", "3"]
stages.p: Split text into item names. Items are separated by any mix of commas and spaces.

stages.l:
match() with g gives you the matched strings but loses the groups. text.matchAll(pattern) gives you every match with its groups. The pattern must have the g flag.

const text = "orc:5 bat:2";
for (const m of text.matchAll(/(\w+):(\d+)/g)) {
  console.log(m[1], Number(m[2]));
}
orc 5
bat 2

Remember that ( and ) are special, so a real bracket is \(.
stages.p: Find every (x,y) in text and return an array of [x, y] number pairs.

stages.l:
m[1] and m[2] get confusing in bigger patterns. A named group gives a group a name: (?<name>...). You read it from m.groups.name.

const m = "x=4 y=9".match(/x=(?<x>\d+) y=(?<y>\d+)/);
console.log(m.groups.x, m.groups.y);
4 9
stages.p: Find a time like 12:05 in text. Return { min: 12, sec: 5 } with numbers, or null if there's no time.
stages.h: /(?<min>\d+):(?<sec>\d+)/, then return { min: Number(m.groups.min), sec: Number(m.groups.sec) }

stages.l:
Now combine anchors, classes and counts to check a whole string. Read this one piece by piece:

/^[A-Z]\d{2}$/
//  ^        start
//  [A-Z]    one capital letter
//  \d{2}    exactly two digits
//  $        end

It matches "B12" but not "B123" or "b12".
stages.p: A valid name is 3 to 12 characters long, uses only letters, digits and _, and starts with a letter. Return true or false.

stages.l:
Lots of games read commands from chat. A regex can split a line into the command name and the rest in one go:

const m = "/kick Bob".match(/^\/(\w+)\s*(.*)$/);
// m[1] is "kick", m[2] is "Bob"

\/ is a real slash, (\w+) grabs the name, \s* skips spaces, and (.*) grabs everything left (maybe nothing).
stages.p: If text starts with /, return { cmd, args }: the command name and an array of the words after it. Otherwise return null.
stages.h: After matching, m[2] might be "". Use m[2] ? m[2].trim().split(/\s+/) : [] for the args.

stages.l:
Tabletop games write dice like 2d6+3: roll 2 six-sided dice and add 3. The count is optional (d20 means one die) and so is the bonus. A pattern for it:

/^(\d*)d(\d+)([+-]\d+)?$/
  • (\d*): count, maybe empty
  • d(\d+): the letter d, then the sides
  • ([+-]\d+)?: an optional plus or minus and a number

Number("+3") is 3 and Number("-2") is -2, so the bonus group converts nicely.
stages.p: Return { count, sides, bonus } as numbers, or null if text isn't valid dice. Missing count means 1, missing bonus means 0.
stages.h: Groups that didn't match are undefined and (\d*) can be "". Use m[1] ? Number(m[1]) : 1 and m[3] ? Number(m[3]) : 0

stages.l:
Time to use everything at once. Game servers write log files, one event per line, like this:

[12:01] INFO Game started
[12:02] WARN Low hp
[12:05] ERROR Boss crashed

Real logs also contain junk lines, so your pattern should only accept lines with exactly the right shape. (INFO|WARN|ERROR) means "one of these words": the | means "or".
stages.p: Split log into lines. For each line shaped like [HH:MM] LEVEL message (two-digit hours and minutes, level INFO, WARN or ERROR), collect { time, level, msg }. Skip every other line. Return the array.
